newsitem.title: UK: Pearson buys U.S. publisher from MCA.
newsitem.headline: Pearson buys U.S. publisher from MCA.

text.p: International media group Pearson, owner of Penguin books, said on Tuesday it had created a publishing powerhouse through its $336 million acquisition of Putnam Berkley in the United States.
The move adds contemporary writers such as Tom Clancy, Patricia Cornwell and Kurt Vonnegut to Penguin's powerful back catalogue of authors and established titles.
"The combination of Penguin and Putnam will create a powerhouse in both the frontlist and backlist," Penguin Group chief executive designate Michael Lynton told Reuters.

Britain's Pearson, whose media empire includes the Financial Times newspaper and the makers of Australian television soap opera Neighbours, bought Putnam Berkley from MCA Inc, the entertainment arm of Canada-based Seagram Co.

It said the acquisition would be earnings enhancing from the first year. It will make Penguin the second largest publisher of English language trade books in the world and the third largest in the U.S. where its market share will double from six percent.

"Because Penguin USA and Putnam are of a like size there is tremendous potential for cost savings," added Lynton, the former head of Disney's Hollywood Pictures who will take over as boss of Penguin at the turn of the year.
Parent company Pearson is also in a state of transition. Texan Marjorie Scardino will take over as chief executive in January, the first woman to head a leading British firm.

Share analysts are scrutinising every move Pearson makes for clues as to the course the company will follow under Scardino as it seeks to focus its activities more tightly. Price reaction was muted, with Pearson shares adding 5p to 755p in a firmer market before slipping back to 751p.

"Is it a signal that Pearson is building in areas where it has a strong position but where there are not particularly attractive long-term growth prospects?" asked Anthony de Larrinaga of Panmure Gordon.
However, Lynton said he was confident about the prospects for the book market.
"In this world of changing technologies, books appear to be a constant. I'm pretty bullish about the situation."
His enthusiasm was not initially shared by Standard & Poor's, which said it might cut Pearson's debt ratings, citing the "negative financial impact of the deal".

Pearson has a mixed record with recent acquisitions and is still trying to turn around U.S. consumer software company Mindscape, which has plunged into loss following its purchase in a $462 million deal in 1994.

Pearson finance director John Makinson said the company was "more than comfortable with the price" paid for Putnam, which had net sales of $276 million and operating profit of $34 million in its last financial year.
He said that the purchase left Pearson with plenty of room for manoeuvre. "I don't think that the size of this acquisition precludes us from doing something else," he said.
